title: CSTM Technical Interview Questions
description: This assessment is designed to support revision and knowledge validation for candidates preparing for their CSTM technical interview. Note that these questions are asked in a 15 minute viva (interview) format in the actual exam.

questions.question: What is Root Squashing?

options.A: A Linux kernel hardening feature that disables all setuid binaries.
options.B: A DNS control that prevents zone transfers from unauthorized hosts.
options.C: A container isolation technique that forces root inside a container to map to root on the host.
options.D: An NFS feature that maps requests from the remote root user to an unprivileged user to prevent root-level access on the server.

questions.explanation: On NFS exports, root squashing reduces risk by preventing the client’s root account from being treated as root on the NFS server.

questions.question: Explain how run0 and the polkit can be used as a more secure alternative to sudo on Linux platforms.

options.A: They encrypt commands in transit so attackers cannot intercept sudo passwords over SSH.
options.B: They are used only for container escape prevention and do not relate to privilege elevation.
options.C: They allow fine-grained, policy-based privilege elevation for specific actions via polkit rules, reducing blanket shell access compared to broad sudo grants.
options.D: They replace PAM entirely and remove the need for authentication for administrative tasks.

questions.explanation: polkit authorizes discrete privileged actions based on rules; tools like run0 can request those actions without granting users unrestricted root shells.

questions.question: What is DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance)?

options.A: A method for compressing email headers to reduce spam filtering overhead.
options.B: A DNS record type used to delegate subdomains securely to third parties.
options.C: An email authentication policy and reporting standard that builds on SPF and DKIM to help receivers handle spoofed mail and provide feedback reports.
options.D: A symmetric encryption protocol for securing SMTP sessions end-to-end.

questions.explanation: DMARC ties SPF/DKIM alignment to a domain policy (none/quarantine/reject) and enables aggregate/forensic reporting.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Sender Policy Framework (SPF)?

options.A: To sign outbound email content with a private key so recipients can validate integrity.
options.B: To encrypt email at rest on the recipient’s mail server.
options.C: To block all inbound mail that contains links or attachments.
options.D: To publish which mail servers are authorized to send email for a domain via DNS, helping prevent sender spoofing.

questions.explanation: SPF lets receivers check the sending IP against a domain’s authorized senders listed in DNS TXT records.

questions.question: What is the purpose of DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)?

options.A: To enforce mandatory TLS between all mail relays on the internet.
options.B: To publish allowed sender IP ranges for a domain in DNS.
options.C: To prevent users from forwarding mail without breaking authentication.
options.D: To cryptographically sign email with a domain key so recipients can verify message integrity and that it was authorized by the domain.

questions.explanation: DKIM adds a signature header that recipients validate using the domain’s public key in DNS.

questions.question: What are the security issues with the FTP protocol?

options.A: Credentials and data are typically transmitted in cleartext, making them vulnerable to interception and manipulation.
options.B: It is UDP-based and therefore cannot be filtered by firewalls.
options.C: It cannot support authentication, so anonymous access is mandatory.
options.D: It provides end-to-end encryption by default but is susceptible to key reuse.

questions.explanation: Classic FTP lacks encryption and is susceptible to sniffing, credential theft, and certain command/data channel abuses; use FTPS or SFTP instead.

questions.question: What is Kerberos?

options.A: A VPN tunneling protocol that encapsulates IP packets.
options.B: A password hashing scheme used by Windows to store credentials.
options.C: A public key infrastructure used to issue TLS certificates for web servers.
options.D: A ticket-based network authentication protocol that uses a trusted Key Distribution Center (KDC) to provide mutual authentication.

questions.explanation: Kerberos uses time-limited tickets (TGT/service tickets) to authenticate users and services without repeatedly sending passwords.

questions.question: Explain directory traversal exploitation

options.A: Injecting SQL meta-characters to extract database rows.
options.B: Manipulating path input (e.g., ../) to access files outside the intended directory, potentially reading sensitive files or executing unintended resources.
options.C: Abusing DNS recursion to enumerate internal hosts.
options.D: Forcing the application to reuse a session token created by another user.

questions.explanation: Traversal exploits insufficient path validation/normalization and can expose configuration files, source code, or credentials.

questions.question: What are the four types of Application Programming Interface (API)?

options.A: REST, SOAP, RPC, and GraphQL.
options.B: TCP, UDP, ICMP, and ARP.
options.C: SQL, NoSQL, LDAP, and SMB.
options.D: Public (open), Partner, Private (internal), and Composite APIs.

questions.explanation: A common high-level classification is by audience/composition: public, partner, private/internal, and composite APIs.

questions.question: How would you fingerprint a database server?

options.A: Only by cracking the database administrator password and logging in.
options.B: By checking the web server’s TLS certificate issuer.
options.C: By using ARP spoofing to force the server to reveal its database type.
options.D: Enumerate banners/version via service probes, review error messages and protocol responses, and validate with authenticated queries where permitted.

questions.explanation: DB fingerprinting typically combines network probing, banner grabbing, error-based hints, and, if allowed, authenticated introspection queries.

questions.question: Explain symmetrical and asymmetrical cryptography

options.A: They are identical; the terms refer to different cipher modes.
options.B: Symmetric uses public keys only; asymmetric uses passwords only.
options.C: Symmetric uses the same key for encryption/decryption; asymmetric uses a public/private key pair for encryption, signatures, and key exchange.
options.D: Symmetric is slower and used only for signatures; asymmetric is faster and used for bulk data.

questions.explanation: Symmetric crypto is efficient for bulk data; asymmetric enables identity binding and key establishment but is computationally heavier.

questions.question: What is the difference between SQL and no SQL database vulnerabilities?

options.A: NoSQL vulnerabilities only relate to buffer overflows in the kernel.
options.B: SQL systems commonly face SQL injection via query concatenation; NoSQL can face NoSQL injection through unvalidated query objects/operators and may differ in auth/ACL models.
options.C: SQL databases cannot be attacked remotely because they only run locally.
options.D: NoSQL databases are immune to injection attacks by design.

questions.explanation: Both can suffer injection, but payloads and query semantics differ (e.g., SQL syntax vs JSON/operator injection).

questions.question: What is the Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL)?

options.A: A protocol for securely transporting vulnerability scan results over TLS.
options.B: A penetration testing methodology framework for web applications.
options.C: A vulnerability scoring system that replaces CVSS.
options.D: A standard for representing and exchanging security configuration and vulnerability checks in a machine-readable way.

questions.explanation: OVAL provides a structured format for security content (definitions, tests, states) used by assessment tools.

questions.question: Explain the difference between Phishing, Smishing and Vishing and what risks do they pose?

options.A: They are all technical exploits with no user interaction required.
options.B: Smishing is email-based and phishing is SMS-based; vishing is social media-based.
options.C: Phishing is only for credential theft; smishing is only for malware; vishing is only for DDoS.
options.D: Phishing uses email, smishing uses SMS/messages, and vishing uses voice calls; all aim to trick users into revealing data, installing malware, or authorizing fraud.

questions.explanation: They are delivery channels for social engineering that can lead to credential compromise, account takeover, and financial loss.

questions.question: What tools could you use to enumerate Domain Name System (DNS) for ZONE transfer vulnerabilities?

options.A: tcpdump and Wireshark only; DNS cannot be queried directly.
options.B: dig, nslookup, and specialized tools like dnsrecon or fierce to attempt AXFR against authoritative name servers.
options.C: hashcat and john; zone transfers require password cracking.
options.D: nmap only; DNS servers do not support zone transfers.

questions.explanation: Attempting AXFR with dig/nslookup and using recon tooling can identify misconfigured authoritative servers permitting zone transfers.

questions.question: Explain what a Security identifier (SID) is and the different parts of a SID.

options.A: A Windows identifier for users/groups: revision, identifier authority, and one or more subauthorities (including domain SID and RID).
options.B: A Linux file permission string made of owner/group/other bits.
options.C: A Kerberos ticket field that stores session keys and timestamps.
options.D: A DNS record that maps hostnames to IPv4 addresses.

questions.explanation: SIDs uniquely identify principals; the final subauthority is typically the RID, appended to the domain SID.

questions.question: What are the two IPsec encoding methods and what are the pros and cons of each?

options.A: RSA and AES; RSA is slower but more secure than AES.
options.B: Transport mode (protects payload; less overhead) and Tunnel mode (encapsulates entire IP packet; better for gateway-to-gateway/VPNs but more overhead).
options.C: Cleartext and Encrypted; cleartext is faster but equally secure.
options.D: Base64 and Hex; Base64 is smaller but less secure than Hex.

questions.explanation: IPsec modes trade off coverage and overhead: transport for host-to-host payload protection; tunnel for network-to-network encapsulation.

questions.question: In key signing do you use the private or public key for signing?

options.A: The public key is used to sign; the private key is used to verify.
options.B: Both keys must be combined to sign a message.
options.C: The private key is used to create the signature; the public key is used to verify it.
options.D: Neither key is used; signing uses only hashing.

questions.explanation: Digital signatures are generated with the signer’s private key and verified with the corresponding public key.

questions.question: What ports need to be open on a domain controller (DC)?

options.A: Only TCP 22 for SSH administration.
options.B: Only TCP 80 and 443 for web-based authentication.
options.C: Only UDP 161 for SNMP monitoring.
options.D: Core services include Kerberos (88), LDAP (389/636), DNS (53), SMB/RPC (445 plus RPC dynamic ports), and often Global Catalog (3268/3269).

questions.explanation: DCs require multiple ports for AD DS, authentication, name resolution, and replication; exact requirements vary by topology but include DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, and SMB/RPC.

questions.question: Explain the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) protocol and any weaknesses in the protocol

options.A: SNMP is used only for email routing and is encrypted by default.
options.B: SNMP cannot be queried remotely, so it has no practical weaknesses.
options.C: SNMP is for monitoring/management; weaknesses include plaintext community strings in v1/v2c and weak/default credentials; v3 improves with auth/privacy but can be misconfigured.
options.D: SNMP is a file transfer protocol with no authentication.

questions.explanation: v1/v2c rely on community strings and are often exposed; v3 adds security features but still depends on strong configuration and access control.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between symmetrical and asymmetrical cryptography?

options.A: Symmetric is fast for bulk encryption but requires secure key sharing; asymmetric simplifies key distribution and supports signatures but is slower and used mainly for key exchange/authentication.
options.B: Asymmetric is always faster and preferred for encrypting large files.
options.C: There are no trade-offs; both have identical performance and properties.
options.D: Symmetric provides non-repudiation; asymmetric does not.

questions.explanation: Most systems use hybrid designs: asymmetric for handshake/key exchange, symmetric for data transport due to performance.

questions.question: Explain some vulnerabilities in SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and TLS (Transport Layer Security)?

options.A: The only vulnerability is that TLS cannot support perfect forward secrecy.
options.B: SSL/TLS vulnerabilities only occur at the IP layer, not the application layer.
options.C: TLS is immune to misconfiguration because it auto-selects the best cipher.
options.D: Examples include obsolete protocol versions (SSLv2/v3), weak ciphers, downgrade attacks, poor certificate validation, and implementation bugs (e.g., Heartbleed).

questions.explanation: Risk often comes from legacy versions, misconfiguration, and software flaws; modern practice is to disable old protocols and weak suites and validate certificates properly.

questions.question: Explain the purpose of a Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADUIS) server

options.A: To host web applications behind a reverse proxy.
options.B: To perform DNS zone transfers between authoritative servers.
options.C: To provide centralized AAA (authentication, authorization, accounting) for network access such as VPN, Wi-Fi (802.1X), and dial-in services.
options.D: To encrypt all LAN traffic at Layer 2.

questions.explanation: RADIUS centralizes access control decisions and accounting for network devices and services.

questions.question: Where are passwords stored on server devices?

options.A: Typically as salted hashes in OS-specific stores (e.g., /etc/shadow on Linux; SAM/NTDS.dit for Windows), not as reversible plaintext.
options.B: Only in DNS TXT records for the domain.
options.C: Only inside the BIOS/UEFI firmware on the motherboard.
options.D: Always in plaintext in /etc/passwd on Linux.

questions.explanation: Modern systems store password verifiers (hashes) in protected credential databases/files with access controls; compromise of these stores enables offline attacks.

questions.question: Explain Structured Query Language injection (SQLi)

options.A: A technique to overflow the stack by sending long SQL strings.
options.B: A DNS attack that injects records into a resolver cache.
options.C: A method to bypass TLS encryption by injecting SQL keywords.
options.D: An attack where untrusted input is concatenated into SQL queries, allowing attackers to alter query logic to read/modify data or execute database functions.

questions.explanation: SQLi results from insufficient input validation and lack of parameterized queries; prepared statements mitigate it.

questions.question: If password hashes cannot be cracked can the hashes be used in any way and how would you do this?

options.A: Yes—upload hashes to DNS to gain domain admin automatically.
options.B: Yes—convert the hash into an AES key and decrypt any file on the network.
options.C: No—hashes are useless unless cracked into plaintext.
options.D: Yes—Pass-the-Hash (and related token-based abuses) can authenticate using the hash directly (e.g., NTLM) without recovering the plaintext password.

questions.explanation: Some protocols (notably NTLM) allow using the password hash as an authentication secret; controls include disabling NTLM where possible and enforcing MFA.

questions.question: Explain how a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) exploit works

options.A: It exploits SQL injection to modify database rows directly.
options.B: It tricks an authenticated user’s browser into submitting a state-changing request to a trusted site, leveraging existing session cookies.
options.C: It forces a server to accept malformed TLS certificates.
options.D: It steals passwords by keylogging the user’s keyboard in the browser.

questions.explanation: CSRF relies on ambient credentials (cookies) and missing anti-CSRF tokens or same-site protections on sensitive actions.

questions.question: Explain session hijacking (with respect to web application testing)

options.A: Brute forcing a database admin account until access is granted.
options.B: Forcing a VPN tunnel to renegotiate encryption keys.
options.C: Taking over a valid user session by stealing or predicting session tokens (e.g., via XSS, sniffing, or insecure cookies) and reusing them to impersonate the user.
options.D: Exploiting directory traversal to read server-side source code.

questions.explanation: Session hijacking focuses on session token confidentiality, integrity, and binding (secure cookies, TLS, regeneration, and anti-XSS controls).

questions.question: What is Internet Information Service (IIS)?

options.A: A Linux init system for starting services.
options.B: A VPN protocol for site-to-site tunneling.
options.C: A database engine used for NoSQL document storage.
options.D: Microsoft’s web server platform for hosting websites and web applications on Windows.

questions.explanation: IIS provides HTTP(S) hosting, application pools, and integration with Windows authentication and .NET.

questions.question: Explain baseboard management controller (BMC) Hacking and the Intelligent Platform Management Interface (IPMI)

options.A: Hacking the GPU driver to increase rendering performance.
options.B: Using ARP spoofing to intercept DNS queries on the LAN.
options.C: Attacking out-of-band management interfaces (e.g., IPMI/BMC) to gain hardware-level control, often via weak auth, default creds, exposed services, or firmware flaws.
options.D: Abusing SMTP relays to send unauthenticated email.

questions.explanation: BMC/IPMI compromise can enable remote power control, console access, and credential theft; management planes should be isolated and secured.

questions.question: What are the pros and cons of using the cloud vs on prem (in terms of cyber security)?

options.A: Cloud removes the need for identity management entirely.
options.B: On-prem eliminates insider threats; cloud increases them only.
options.C: Cloud can offer strong baseline controls and rapid patching, but introduces shared-responsibility, misconfiguration risk, and dependency on provider controls; on-prem offers direct control but requires in-house security maturity.
options.D: Cloud is always less secure because it is public; on-prem is always secure.

questions.explanation: Security posture depends on governance and configuration; cloud improves some controls but shifts responsibilities and expands the configuration surface.

questions.question: What technical controls are available in the cloud to help with cyber security?

options.A: Only DNS filtering; other controls are not available.
options.B: IAM policies/MFA, network segmentation (VPC/VNet, security groups), logging/monitoring, encryption/KMS, WAF/DDoS protections, and posture management tools.
options.C: Only physical security at the data center perimeter.
options.D: Only antivirus installed on virtual machines.

questions.explanation: Major clouds provide layered controls for identity, network, data protection, and continuous monitoring, but require correct configuration and governance.

questions.question: What are the most popular containerization solutions?

options.A: Docker and containerd, often orchestrated with Kubernetes; podman is also common as a daemonless alternative.
options.B: Hyper-V and VMware ESXi.
options.C: WEP and WPA2.
options.D: SMTP and IMAP.

questions.explanation: Modern container ecosystems commonly use OCI-compatible runtimes (Docker/containerd/podman) with orchestration via Kubernetes.

questions.question: What’s the difference between virtual machines and containerization?

options.A: VMs cannot be networked; containers can.
options.B: VMs virtualize hardware and run separate OS kernels; containers share the host kernel and isolate processes, making them lighter but with different isolation boundaries.
options.C: Containers are always more secure because they cannot escape.
options.D: Containers require a hypervisor; VMs run directly on the host kernel.

questions.explanation: VMs provide stronger kernel isolation; containers improve efficiency and portability but rely on correct kernel hardening and runtime configuration.

questions.question: What are the signs a mobile device has been jail broken?

options.A: The screen brightness increases automatically at night.
options.B: Presence of root/jailbreak tools (e.g., Cydia/Sileo), unusual privilege escalation apps, disabled sandboxing indicators, or integrity checks failing (e.g., SafetyNet/DeviceCheck).
options.C: The device can connect to Wi‑Fi networks.
options.D: The phone battery lasts longer than normal.

questions.explanation: Jailbreak/rooting often leaves artifacts (package managers, altered system partitions) and breaks platform integrity verification controls.

questions.question: What file types are associated with android apps?

options.A: APK (and the newer AAB for Play distribution), with DEX bytecode inside packages.
options.B: EXE and MSI.
options.C: JAR only; Android does not use packages.
options.D: IPA and DMG.

questions.explanation: Android apps are commonly distributed as APKs; developers may publish AAB bundles that produce device-specific APKs.

questions.question: What file types are associated with apple apps?

options.A: RPM and DEB.
options.B: IPA packages (iOS/iPadOS), and macOS apps commonly as .app bundles or distributed via DMG/PKG installers.
options.C: EXE and BAT.
options.D: APK and AAB.

questions.explanation: Apple platforms use IPA for iOS/iPadOS distribution and app bundles/installers on macOS.

questions.question: Explain the use case for Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS).

options.A: To provide TLS-like encryption and authentication over UDP for latency-sensitive applications (e.g., VoIP, WebRTC) where TCP is unsuitable.
options.B: To compress UDP payloads to improve throughput.
options.C: To route DNS queries anonymously through relays.
options.D: To replace IPsec for encrypting disks at rest.

questions.explanation: DTLS adapts TLS concepts to UDP, handling reordering/loss while securing datagrams.

questions.question: What are the built-in user accounts on a Windows server?

options.A: postgres, mysql, and sa.
options.B: ec2-user and ubuntu.
options.C: Common built-ins include Administrator, Guest (often disabled), and service accounts like LocalSystem, LocalService, and NetworkService.
options.D: root, nobody, and daemon.

questions.explanation: Windows includes default local accounts and well-known service identities used by the OS and services; hardening often involves disabling/renaming where appropriate.

questions.question: Name some protocols in the Industrial control system (ICS) / Operational Technology (OT) space?

options.A: IMAP, POP3, and SMTP only.
options.B: SIP, RTP, and SRTP only.
options.C: BGP, OSPF, and IS-IS only.
options.D: Modbus, DNP3, BACnet, OPC (classic/UA), and PROFINET are common ICS/OT protocols.

questions.explanation: ICS/OT environments use specialized industrial protocols for control and telemetry, many of which were designed without strong security controls.

questions.question: Name some security models and what is the purpose of security models?

options.A: Examples include Bell–LaPadula, Biba, Clark–Wilson, and Brewer–Nash; they formalize security properties and guide system policy/design.
options.B: Examples include RAID levels; they define disk redundancy.
options.C: Examples include TCP/IP and OSI; they define packet formats.
options.D: Examples include AES and RSA; they define encryption algorithms.

questions.explanation: Security models provide formal rules for confidentiality/integrity and help reason about and enforce access control policies.

questions.question: What are the issues with the Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) protocol?

options.A: It uses weak IVs and RC4 key scheduling, enabling practical key recovery and traffic decryption; it is considered broken.
options.B: It mandates AES-256 and therefore is too slow for Wi‑Fi.
options.C: It cannot authenticate clients, so all Wi‑Fi is anonymous.
options.D: It is immune to replay attacks due to perfect forward secrecy.

questions.explanation: WEP’s design flaws allow attackers to capture enough traffic to recover the key; WPA2/WPA3 should be used instead.

questions.question: What are the security issues associated with Lanman (LM) passwords?

options.A: They require smart cards, which are easy to clone.
options.B: They store plaintext passwords in the registry by default.
options.C: They are case-insensitive, split into 7-character chunks, and use weak hashing, making them highly susceptible to brute force and rainbow tables.
options.D: They are salted with modern bcrypt, making cracking infeasible.

questions.explanation: LM hashing dramatically reduces password entropy, accelerating offline cracking and credential compromise.

questions.question: Explain the purpose of the phpMyAdmin application.

options.A: A VPN client for IPsec tunnels.
options.B: A Linux kernel module for memory management.
options.C: A web-based administration interface for MySQL/MariaDB to manage databases, users, and queries.
options.D: A Windows service for domain authentication.

questions.explanation: phpMyAdmin provides convenient DB administration over the web, which must be secured due to its high privilege and attack surface.

questions.question: How would you find and download files from a File Transfer Protocol (FTP) server or a Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) server?

options.A: By querying DNS TXT records for file contents.
options.B: Only by exploiting buffer overflows in the FTP server.
options.C: Enumerate directories/files (e.g., ftp ls/dir; nmap scripts), then retrieve with ftp get/mget or tftp get, respecting authorization and scope.
options.D: By sending ICMP echo requests and reading the payload.

questions.explanation: FTP supports authenticated directory listing and retrieval; TFTP is simpler and often unauthenticated, so exposure can allow easy file downloads.

questions.question: What enumeration can the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) service be used for?

options.A: Enumerating SMB shares and Windows domain SIDs.
options.B: User enumeration (e.g., VRFY/EXPN/RCPT TO behavior), mail relay testing, and banner/version discovery.
options.C: Enumerating wireless networks and WPA handshakes.
options.D: Enumerating database tables via SQL injection.

questions.explanation: SMTP responses can reveal valid recipients and relay configuration; modern servers often disable VRFY/EXPN but misconfigurations persist.

questions.question: What is steganography?

options.A: Hiding information within other data (e.g., images/audio) so the existence of the message is concealed.
options.B: Compressing files to reduce size for transmission.
options.C: Hashing passwords to store them securely.
options.D: Encrypting data so it is unreadable without a key.

questions.explanation: Unlike encryption, steganography aims to conceal that communication is happening at all.

questions.question: What is a relative identifier (RID) Master?

options.A: An Active Directory FSMO role that allocates pools of RIDs to domain controllers so they can create unique SIDs for new objects.
options.B: A Kerberos server that issues ticket-granting tickets.
options.C: A DNS master server that handles zone transfers.
options.D: A Windows service that manages print queues across a forest.

questions.explanation: The RID Master prevents SID collisions by controlling RID allocation used in object SID generation.

questions.question: Explain Hashing functions ie MD5 and SHA1

options.A: They are public key algorithms used for key exchange.
options.B: They are compression algorithms used to shrink files.
options.C: They are symmetric ciphers used to encrypt disks.
options.D: They produce fixed-length digests for integrity; MD5 and SHA‑1 are considered collision-broken and unsuitable for modern security uses like signatures.

questions.explanation: Hash functions map data to a digest; weaknesses in MD5/SHA‑1 enable collision attacks, so stronger hashes (e.g., SHA‑256) are preferred.

questions.question: Explain with examples some protocols used for Wide Area Networks (WAN)

options.A: NFS, SMB, and AFP.
options.B: Examples include MPLS, PPP/PPPoE, Frame Relay (legacy), and BGP for interdomain routing.
options.C: WEP, WPA2, and WPA3.
options.D: USB, HDMI, and PCIe.

questions.explanation: WAN protocols/technologies support long-distance connectivity and routing; some are legacy while others (MPLS/BGP) remain common.

questions.question: What is a One-Time-Pad?

options.A: A public key certificate used to sign software.
options.B: A cipher using a truly random key as long as the message, used once; when used correctly it provides information-theoretic security.
options.C: A password policy requiring users to change passwords weekly.
options.D: A disk encryption mode that reuses the same key for all files.

questions.explanation: OTP security depends on truly random, same-length keys, single use, and secure key distribution—practicality is the main challenge.

questions.question: What is a Schema Master?

options.A: A Windows service that manages DHCP leases.
options.B: A Kerberos role that stores user passwords in plaintext.
options.C: An Active Directory FSMO role that controls updates to the AD schema, ensuring only one DC processes schema modifications at a time.
options.D: A DNS role that authoritatively resolves all internet domains.

questions.explanation: Schema changes are forest-wide; the Schema Master coordinates them to avoid inconsistent schema replication.

questions.question: Explain null sessions and restrict anonymous settings

options.A: Restrict anonymous settings disable all user authentication on a domain.
options.B: Null sessions occur only on Wi‑Fi networks using WEP.
options.C: Null sessions are encrypted TLS tunnels that improve privacy.
options.D: Null sessions are unauthenticated SMB connections that can expose information; restrict anonymous settings limit what anonymous users can enumerate over SMB/NetBIOS.

questions.explanation: Hardening typically involves disabling legacy anonymous enumeration and tightening SMB/RPC access controls.

questions.question: What vulnerability might be present if Server Message Block (SMB) version 1 was enabled on a Windows device?

options.A: Exposure to legacy SMBv1 flaws and exploit chains (e.g., vulnerabilities leveraged by wormable attacks), plus weaker security features compared to SMBv2/v3.
options.B: It disables file sharing entirely, preventing any access.
options.C: It forces all traffic onto UDP, enabling amplification attacks only.
options.D: It automatically enables MFA for all users, which attackers can bypass.

questions.explanation: SMBv1 is obsolete and lacks modern protections; it should be disabled in favor of SMBv2/v3 where possible.

questions.question: Explain the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model

options.A: A database normalization model for structuring tables.
options.B: A symmetric encryption model for key distribution.
options.C: A 7-layer conceptual model (Physical to Application) that standardizes how network functions are layered and interact.
options.D: A 3-layer model used only for cloud security.

questions.explanation: The OSI model helps reason about protocols, troubleshooting, and where security controls operate across layers 1–7.

questions.question: Explain the Department of Defense (DoD) networking model

options.A: A 4-layer model (Link, Internet, Transport, Application) similar to TCP/IP that describes network communications in broader layers.
options.B: A vulnerability scoring model used by CVSS.
options.C: A 7-layer model identical to OSI.
options.D: A wireless-only model for WPA authentication.

questions.explanation: The DoD/TCP-IP model groups functions into fewer layers than OSI, commonly used to describe internet protocol stacks.

questions.question: Explain how Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) works

options.A: It resolves domain names to IP addresses using recursive queries.
options.B: It authenticates users to a domain controller using tickets.
options.C: It encrypts network traffic between hosts using shared keys.
options.D: It automatically assigns IP configuration using a DORA process (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) and leases addresses for a period.

questions.explanation: DHCP centralizes IP allocation and options (gateway, DNS); attacks include rogue DHCP and starvation without protections.

questions.question: What is a Start of Authority (SOA) record - with respect to Domain Name System (DNS)?

options.A: A DNS record that contains authoritative information about a zone, including the primary name server, admin contact, and serial/refresh timers.
options.B: A DNS record that indicates a mail exchanger for the domain.
options.C: A DNS record that maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.
options.D: A DNS record that stores a public key for DKIM signing.

questions.explanation: SOA defines zone authority and controls replication/refresh behavior via timers and serial number.

questions.question: Explain what Domain Name System (DNS) is and explain how DNS works.

options.A: A protocol that assigns IP addresses dynamically to clients.
options.B: A transport protocol that provides reliable delivery over IP.
options.C: A firewall technology that blocks malicious domains by default.
options.D: A hierarchical naming system that maps domain names to records (A/AAAA/CNAME/MX, etc.) using recursive resolvers querying authoritative servers with caching.

questions.explanation: DNS queries flow from client to resolver to authoritative servers, with caching to improve performance; security issues include spoofing and misconfiguration.

questions.question: Explain the IP protocol and explain IP addresses.

options.A: IP routes packets across networks using source/destination IP addresses; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.
options.B: IP encrypts packets end-to-end by default.
options.C: IP addresses are MAC addresses formatted with colons.
options.D: IP is an application-layer protocol for web pages.

questions.explanation: IP is a network-layer protocol providing best-effort delivery and addressing for routing across interconnected networks.

questions.question: Explain Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)

options.A: A protocol that replaces TCP with a faster transport.
options.B: A method of IP addressing and routing using variable-length prefixes (e.g., /24) to allocate and aggregate address space efficiently.
options.C: A technique to hide web traffic inside DNS queries.
options.D: A Wi‑Fi security standard that supersedes WPA3.

questions.explanation: CIDR replaced classful addressing, enabling flexible subnetting and route aggregation using prefix lengths.

questions.question: Explain how Machine-in-the-Middle (MITM) techniques work with the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP).

options.A: By changing BGP routes on the public internet without access to the LAN.
options.B: By exploiting DNSSEC signatures to change records.
options.C: By brute forcing WPA passwords over the air.
options.D: By poisoning ARP caches so victims map an IP to the attacker’s MAC, allowing interception/relay of traffic on a LAN segment.

questions.explanation: ARP lacks authentication; forged ARP replies can redirect traffic through an attacker, mitigated by protections like static ARP, DHCP snooping, and DAI.

questions.question: What is the function of Port Address Translation (PAT)?

options.A: To allocate DNS zones to authoritative servers.
options.B: To allow many internal hosts to share a single public IP by translating internal addresses/ports to external ports (a form of NAT).
options.C: To route packets based on MAC addresses only.
options.D: To encrypt TCP ports so scanners cannot detect services.

questions.explanation: PAT multiplexes sessions using port numbers, conserving public IPv4 space and enabling outbound connectivity from private networks.

questions.question: What is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)?

options.A: A file transfer protocol that runs only over UDP.
options.B: A time synchronization protocol for network devices.
options.C: A protocol for accessing and managing directory services (e.g., Active Directory), used for querying users, groups, and objects.
options.D: A routing protocol that selects paths between routers.

questions.explanation: LDAP provides a standardized way to query directory information; insecure binds and misconfigurations can expose credentials and data.

questions.question: Name and explain two distance vector routing protocols

options.A: RIP and EIGRP (often treated as advanced DV): they exchange route information with neighbors based on distance/metric rather than full topology.
options.B: ARP and ICMP; they compute shortest paths across WANs.
options.C: OSPF and IS‑IS; they are distance vector protocols.
options.D: BGP and HTTP; they exchange routes over the web.

questions.explanation: Distance vector protocols propagate route metrics to neighbors; they can be simpler but may converge slower and be susceptible to routing loops.

questions.question: Explain Medium Access Control (MAC) addresses and explain what an Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) is?

options.A: A MAC is an IP address; an OUI is the DNS zone name.
options.B: A MAC is a port number; an OUI is a routing metric.
options.C: A MAC is a Layer 2 hardware address; the OUI is the first 24 bits identifying the manufacturer (or assignment) of the network interface.
options.D: A MAC is a user ID; an OUI is a password hash.

questions.explanation: MAC addresses identify interfaces on a local network; OUIs are assigned blocks used in MAC addressing and can aid device identification.

questions.question: What is firewalking (with respect to network security)?

options.A: A technique for exploiting SQL injection to enumerate tables.
options.B: A technique to infer firewall rules by sending packets with crafted TTL values to determine which ports/protocols are permitted through a filtering device.
options.C: A physical security test of sprinkler systems and fire doors.
options.D: A method to crack WPA2 by capturing handshakes.

questions.explanation: Firewalking leverages hop counts and ICMP responses to map permitted traffic through packet filters.

questions.question: Explain the Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA) protocol

options.A: A file transfer protocol used for downloading firmware.
options.B: A wireless security standard improving on WEP; WPA uses TKIP (legacy) and WPA2 uses AES-CCMP, while WPA3 further improves key exchange and protection.
options.C: A routing protocol for exchanging routes between autonomous systems.
options.D: An email authentication method based on DNS TXT records.

questions.explanation: WPA family protocols secure Wi‑Fi by providing authentication and encryption; WPA2/WPA3 are preferred over legacy WPA/TKIP.

questions.question: Explain IPSec

options.A: A DNS protocol that ensures integrity of DNS records.
options.B: A suite that secures IP traffic with authentication and encryption using AH/ESP, often for VPNs, operating in transport or tunnel mode.
options.C: A TCP option that increases window size for performance.
options.D: A web application firewall that blocks SQL injection.

questions.explanation: IPsec provides confidentiality/integrity at the network layer and is commonly used for site-to-site and remote-access VPNs.

questions.question: Where would you find the hosts file and what is its purpose of this file?

options.A: It is stored only on DNS servers and defines authoritative zones.
options.B: It is stored in the browser cache and defines TLS certificates.
options.C: It is stored in the router firmware and defines NAT rules.
options.D: It is a local name-to-IP mapping file (e.g., /etc/hosts on Unix-like systems; %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\etc\hosts on Windows) that overrides DNS resolution.

questions.explanation: The hosts file provides static resolution entries and is consulted before (or alongside) DNS, enabling overrides and sometimes abuse via tampering.

questions.question: Explain how Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANS) work

options.A: VLANs are Layer 3 routing protocols that replace IP.
options.B: VLANs encrypt Wi‑Fi frames so attackers cannot sniff traffic.
options.C: VLANs logically segment Layer 2 networks by tagging frames (802.1Q) so devices can be separated into distinct broadcast domains on the same physical infrastructure.
options.D: VLANs are only for connecting remote sites over the internet.

questions.explanation: VLAN tagging allows separation of traffic and reduces broadcast scope; inter-VLAN communication requires routing and appropriate ACLs.

questions.question: Explain the purpose of a Terminal Access Controller Access Control System (TACACS)

options.A: A protocol for synchronizing time across servers.
options.B: A tunneling protocol for encrypting IP traffic over UDP.
options.C: A protocol for discovering devices on a local network.
options.D: A centralized AAA protocol (commonly TACACS+) for authenticating and authorizing administrative access to network devices, with detailed command accounting.

questions.explanation: TACACS+ is often used for device administration (routers/switches) and supports granular authorization and accounting.

questions.question: Why are CLOSED ports a cause for concern?

options.A: Closed ports always indicate malware is present.
options.B: Closed ports mean the firewall blocks all traffic so there is no risk.
options.C: Closed ports reveal the encryption keys used by the host.
options.D: They indicate a reachable host and an IP stack responding, which can aid attacker reconnaissance and may reflect unnecessary exposure even if no service is listening.

questions.explanation: Closed ports can still provide information (host up, TCP/IP fingerprinting) and may signal services that are intermittently available or misconfigured filtering.

questions.question: How would you set a source port in nmap and why would you use this feature?

options.A: Use --spoof-mac to change the source port at Layer 2.
options.B: Use -p to set the destination port, which is the same as the source port.
options.C: Use --source-port (or -g) to set a specific source port, sometimes to bypass poorly configured ACLs that trust traffic from certain ports (e.g., 53).
options.D: You cannot set a source port in nmap.

questions.explanation: Some legacy filters allow traffic based on source port; setting it can test for such weaknesses, though it is not a reliable bypass against stateful controls.

questions.question: Explain the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) protocol

options.A: A Layer 2/3 mapping protocol used on LANs to resolve an IP address to a MAC address via broadcasts and replies.
options.B: A routing protocol used to exchange routes between routers.
options.C: A transport protocol that guarantees reliable delivery.
options.D: An application protocol used to send emails.

questions.explanation: ARP enables local delivery on Ethernet by mapping IPs to MACs; its lack of authentication enables ARP spoofing.

questions.question: Explain the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) protocol

options.A: A protocol used to encrypt HTTP traffic.
options.B: A network-layer protocol used for diagnostic and control messages (e.g., ping echo, destination unreachable, time exceeded).
options.C: A database protocol for executing queries.
options.D: A Layer 2 protocol for switching frames.

questions.explanation: ICMP supports troubleshooting and error reporting; it can be abused for reconnaissance or tunneling if not controlled appropriately.

questions.question: Explain the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) protocol

options.A: A protocol that replaces IP addressing with MAC addressing.
options.B: A connectionless transport protocol providing best-effort delivery without retransmissions, used for low-latency services like DNS and VoIP.
options.C: A connection-oriented protocol that guarantees in-order delivery.
options.D: A routing protocol for exchanging BGP updates.

questions.explanation: UDP trades reliability for reduced overhead and latency; applications must handle loss/reordering if needed.

questions.question: What are the response codes for the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (http) protocol?

options.A: Status code classes: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
options.B: Only 200 and 404 are valid HTTP responses.
options.C: HTTP response codes are MAC addresses.
options.D: HTTP uses DNS response codes like NXDOMAIN and SERVFAIL.

questions.explanation: HTTP status codes indicate the outcome of a request, grouped by class to quickly convey the type of result or error.

questions.question: Explain IPV6 and why its not widely adopted

options.A: IPv6 cannot be routed on the internet.
options.B: IPv6 is a proprietary protocol requiring paid licenses.
options.C: IPv6 uses 128-bit addressing to solve IPv4 exhaustion; slower adoption is due to legacy infrastructure, cost/complexity, and continued IPv4 via NAT.
options.D: IPv6 reduces address space compared to IPv4.

questions.explanation: IPv6 adoption is increasing but uneven; operational inertia and IPv4 NAT workarounds slowed migration despite address exhaustion pressures.

questions.question: What are the two IPSec Modes

options.A: Client mode and Server mode.
options.B: WEP mode and WPA mode.
options.C: Inline mode and Offline mode.
options.D: Transport mode and Tunnel mode.

questions.explanation: IPsec operates either by protecting the payload (transport) or encapsulating the entire packet (tunnel).

questions.question: What is the Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS) protocol?

options.A: A protocol for transferring files securely over SSH.
options.B: A protocol for authenticating users to Active Directory.
options.C: A link-state interior gateway routing protocol used within an autonomous system, common in service provider networks.
options.D: A protocol for resolving hostnames to IP addresses.

questions.explanation: IS-IS exchanges topology information to compute shortest paths, similar in concept to OSPF but with different encapsulation and deployment patterns.

questions.question: Explain the Network File System (NFS) protocol

options.A: A VPN protocol for encrypting IP packets.
options.B: A routing protocol used to exchange routes.
options.C: A distributed file system protocol allowing clients to access remote files over a network as if local, common in Unix/Linux environments.
options.D: A protocol for sending emails between mail servers.

questions.explanation: NFS enables shared storage; security depends on version/configuration (e.g., auth, exports, and use of Kerberos).

questions.question: Explain the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Protocol

options.A: A protocol used to scan open ports on a host.
options.B: A protocol used by IPsec to negotiate Security Associations and establish keys (IKEv1/IKEv2) for secure tunnels.
options.C: A protocol used to allocate IP addresses dynamically.
options.D: A protocol used to retrieve email from a mailbox.

questions.explanation: IKE handles authentication and key agreement for IPsec, setting up parameters and keys for ESP/AH.

questions.question: What protocols are associated with Virtual Private Network (VPN)?

options.A: POP3, IMAP, and NNTP.
options.B: Common VPN-related protocols include IPsec/IKE, SSL/TLS VPNs (e.g., OpenVPN), and WireGuard.
options.C: HTTP, FTP, and SMTP.
options.D: ARP, ICMP, and IGMP.

questions.explanation: VPNs typically rely on tunneling and cryptographic protocols such as IPsec or TLS-based tunnels; modern options include WireGuard.

questions.question: What protocols are associated with Voice over Internet Protocol (VOIP)?

options.A: BGP for routing and OSPF for link-state updates.
options.B: NFS for network storage and SNMP for monitoring.
options.C: SMB for file sharing and LDAP for directory queries.
options.D: SIP for signaling, RTP/RTCP for media transport, and often SRTP/TLS for securing media/signaling.

questions.explanation: VoIP commonly uses SIP for call setup and RTP for audio/video streams, with secure variants for confidentiality and integrity.

questions.question: Name and explain a Kerberos exploit?

options.A: Kerberoasting: requesting service tickets for SPNs and cracking the ticket offline to recover weak service account passwords.
options.B: SQL injection: altering database queries via input.
options.C: Heartbleed: reading memory from vulnerable TLS servers.
options.D: ARP spoofing: poisoning a LAN to intercept packets.

questions.explanation: Kerberoasting abuses the ability to request service tickets and perform offline password cracking against service account secrets.

questions.question: What is a Pre-Shared Key (PSK) used for and what are the issues with its use?

options.A: A shared secret used for authentication/key derivation (e.g., WPA2-PSK); issues include sharing at scale, weak passphrases, and no per-user accountability.
options.B: A routing key used by BGP; issues include path hijacking.
options.C: A public certificate used to validate server identity; issues include certificate pinning.
options.D: A hardware token used for MFA; issues include battery life.

questions.explanation: PSKs are simple but create shared-risk: compromise affects all users, and weak PSKs are susceptible to offline dictionary attacks (e.g., Wi‑Fi handshakes).

questions.question: How many versions of the Network File System (NFS) protocol are there and what is the compatibility between the versions?

options.A: There are 10 versions and they are all fully interchangeable.
options.B: Commonly referenced versions are NFSv2, NFSv3, and NFSv4 (with v4.1/v4.2); v4 is not fully backward compatible with v2/v3 semantics and often uses different ports/behavior.
options.C: Only one version exists; all implementations are identical.
options.D: NFS has only v1 and v2, both deprecated and incompatible with TCP.

questions.explanation: NFS evolved across major versions; compatibility depends on client/server support, and v4 introduces significant architectural/security changes compared to v2/v3.

questions.question: How do you mitigate Server Message Block (SMB) issues?

options.A: Disable all logging to improve performance.
options.B: Disable SMBv1, enforce SMB signing where appropriate, restrict exposure (firewall/segmentation), apply patches, and use least privilege on shares.
options.C: Enable anonymous SMB access to reduce authentication failures.
options.D: Expose SMB directly to the internet to simplify access.

questions.explanation: SMB hardening focuses on removing legacy versions, limiting access paths, patching, and enforcing integrity controls like signing.

questions.question: How do you mitigate an external facing Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) server with an expired Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate?

options.A: Disable encryption so certificate validation is bypassed.
options.B: Replace/renew the certificate, enforce modern TLS settings, restrict internet exposure (VPN/zero trust), and enable MFA/conditional access.
options.C: Move RDP to port 80 to blend with web traffic.
options.D: Ignore the certificate; RDP does not use TLS.

questions.explanation: Expired certs undermine trust and may enable downgrade/impersonation risks; proper certificate management and reducing exposure are key mitigations.

questions.question: How do you mitigate machine in the middle (MITM) attacks?

options.A: Disable TLS to reduce complexity.
options.B: Use shared accounts to simplify access control.
options.C: Use strong encryption with certificate validation (TLS), secure Wi‑Fi, implement network protections (DAI, DHCP snooping), and avoid trusting unvalidated networks.
options.D: Allow ARP replies from any host without monitoring.

questions.explanation: Mitigation combines cryptographic protections and network-layer controls that prevent spoofing/poisoning and enforce authenticity.

questions.question: How do you mitigate Structured Query Language injection (SQLi)?

options.A: Use parameterized queries/prepared statements, input validation, least-privileged DB accounts, and secure error handling; consider WAF as defense-in-depth.
options.B: Concatenate user input after escaping single quotes only.
options.C: Run the database as administrator to avoid permission errors.
options.D: Disable authentication so attackers cannot log in.

questions.explanation: SQLi prevention centers on separating code from data (parameterization) and reducing the impact if flaws occur.

questions.question: How do you mitigate socially engineered staff?

options.A: Share passwords across teams to improve resilience.
options.B: Implement security awareness training, strong verification procedures, least privilege, MFA, and reporting/response processes for suspicious requests.
options.C: Allow unmanaged personal devices to access sensitive systems.
options.D: Disable logging so staff are not monitored.

questions.explanation: Mitigation is procedural and technical: educate users and put controls in place so a single mistake is less likely to cause compromise.

questions.question: How do you mitigate a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability?

options.A: Store user input in base64 so it cannot execute.
options.B: Output encode/escape untrusted data, validate inputs, use Content Security Policy (CSP), and avoid unsafe DOM sinks; set HttpOnly/Secure cookies.
options.C: Use FTP instead of HTTP.
options.D: Disable JavaScript in the browser for all users.

questions.explanation: XSS is mitigated by preventing script injection/execution and limiting impact through CSP and secure session cookie flags.

questions.question: What is the mitigation for a ransomware attack where files have been locked?

options.A: Turn off antivirus permanently to stop alerts.
options.B: Publish the encryption keys to the internet.
options.C: Isolate affected systems, restore from verified offline backups, investigate and eradicate the intrusion, and follow incident response/legal guidance; avoid paying where possible.
options.D: Immediately delete all backups to prevent reinfection.

questions.explanation: Effective mitigation relies on resilient backups and incident response; payment does not guarantee recovery and can fund further crime.

questions.question: What should be in a scope document for a security test?

options.A: Only a list of usernames to use.
options.B: Only the final report template with no constraints.
options.C: Objectives, in/out-of-scope assets, permitted techniques, time windows, points of contact, rules of engagement, data handling, reporting expectations, and approval/sign-off.
options.D: Only the tester’s preferred tools list.

questions.explanation: A robust scope defines what is authorized, boundaries, safety constraints, and communications to ensure lawful, controlled testing.

questions.question: What laws affect security testing?

options.A: Commonly relevant are computer misuse/cybercrime statutes, data protection/privacy laws, interception/surveillance laws, and contractual obligations depending on jurisdiction.
options.B: No laws apply if the test is for security purposes.
options.C: Only maritime law applies to penetration tests.
options.D: Only copyright law applies to all testing activities.

questions.explanation: Security testing must be authorized and comply with applicable cybercrime, privacy, and interception laws as well as contracts and regulations.

questions.question: What risk mitigation can you put in place before conducting a security test?

options.A: Test production systems without notifying anyone to simulate realism.
options.B: Disable backups to reduce storage usage.
options.C: Use default credentials to reduce setup time.
options.D: Obtain written authorization, define ROE, schedule safe windows, set monitoring/rollback plans, back up critical systems, and establish comms/escalation paths.

questions.explanation: Pre-test mitigations reduce operational impact and legal risk by ensuring authorization, readiness, and response plans.

questions.question: What is the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and Common vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE)?

options.A: CVSS identifies people; CVE identifies network devices.
options.B: CVSS is a scoring framework for vulnerability severity; CVE is a catalogue of publicly known vulnerabilities with unique identifiers.
options.C: CVSS is a patching tool; CVE is an encryption algorithm.
options.D: CVSS is a legal standard; CVE is a penetration testing methodology.

questions.explanation: CVE provides naming/IDs for vulnerabilities; CVSS provides a standardized way to rate severity for prioritization.

questions.question: What are the testing regulations regarding CHECK level testing?

options.A: CHECK is a US federal encryption standard for VPNs.
options.B: CHECK is a UK government scheme requiring approved providers/testers and adherence to defined methodologies and reporting for certain public sector testing contexts.
options.C: CHECK is an EU law that bans penetration testing.
options.D: CHECK is a DNS security extension for government domains.

questions.explanation: CHECK-level engagements typically require specific accreditation and process compliance; testers must ensure they meet scheme requirements for applicable work.

questions.question: What part of the Human Rights Act 1998 affects pen testers?

options.A: Article 12 mandates testers disclose all vulnerabilities publicly.
options.B: No part applies because it only covers physical security.
options.C: Rights related to privacy and family life (notably Article 8, via the ECHR) can be relevant when handling personal data and surveillance-like activity.
options.D: Article 1 on property requires all pen tests to be free of charge.

questions.explanation: Testing that touches personal data or monitoring must respect privacy rights and proportionality, reflected in policies and lawful authorization.

questions.question: What is the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA) and does it affect security testing?

options.A: A UK law governing interception and surveillance powers; it can affect testing where communications interception/monitoring is involved and requires proper authority.
options.B: A regulation that defines CVSS scoring.
options.C: A law that mandates MFA for all UK citizens.
options.D: A law that only applies to hardware imports.

questions.explanation: If a test involves intercepting communications, RIPA considerations may apply; proper consent/authorization is critical.

questions.question: What is the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and how does it affect security testing?

options.A: A vulnerability database used by scanners.
options.B: A routing standard for IPv6 adoption.
options.C: An EU/UK data protection framework requiring lawful processing, data minimization, security, and rights protections; pen tests must handle personal data appropriately with agreements and controls.
options.D: A Wi‑Fi encryption protocol.

questions.explanation: Testing often touches personal data; GDPR drives requirements for legal basis, processing agreements, retention limits, and security of test data.

questions.question: Name and explain three security standards

options.A: Examples: HTTP, FTP, and SMTP.
options.B: Examples: WEP, WPA, and WPA3.
options.C: Examples: FAT32, NTFS, and ext4.
options.D: Examples: ISO/IEC 27001 (ISMS), PCI DSS (payment card security), and NIST SP 800-53 (security controls catalogue).

questions.explanation: Standards provide structured requirements/controls for managing and assessing security in specific contexts (general management, payments, control baselines).

questions.question: What are the risks of enumerating and vulnerability assessing a multifunction printing device?

options.A: No risks; printers cannot store data.
options.B: It automatically patches the device and improves security.
options.C: Potential service disruption, exposure of stored documents/credentials, lateral movement via embedded OS, and privacy impacts from captured scans/prints.
options.D: It only risks increasing toner usage.

questions.explanation: MFPs can store sensitive data and run network services; aggressive scanning can cause outages and create privacy/legal concerns if data is accessed.

questions.question: What are the risks of enumerating and vulnerability assessing an ICS device?

options.A: The only risk is increased electricity cost.
options.B: ICS devices are identical to laptops so the risk is the same.
options.C: No risks because ICS protocols are encrypted by default.
options.D: Operational disruption/safety impact, fragile protocols, potential downtime, and legal/contractual consequences due to criticality of OT environments.

questions.explanation: OT devices can be safety-critical and sensitive to scanning; testing must be carefully scoped, coordinated, and often performed with non-intrusive techniques.

questions.question: What is the Police and Justice Act 2006 (PJA) and how does it affect security testing?

options.A: A UK act that amended aspects of computer misuse and related offences; it reinforces the need for explicit authorization and lawful conduct during testing.
options.B: A law that defines wireless encryption requirements for Wi‑Fi.
options.C: A law that only applies to physical penetration testing.
options.D: A regulation that requires all scans be run from London.

questions.explanation: Legal frameworks around unauthorized access and impairment mean penetration testing must be properly authorized and controlled to avoid criminal liability.

questions.question: Explain how to keep to scope during a security test.

options.A: Scan any system you can reach to maximize coverage.
options.B: Avoid documenting actions to reduce evidence.
options.C: Follow the agreed ROE, target only authorized assets, use allowlists, document actions, stop/escalate on unexpected access, and maintain continuous communication with stakeholders.
options.D: Exploit high-risk findings on unrelated systems to prove impact.

questions.explanation: Scope discipline is maintained through technical guardrails and process: asset lists, approvals, logging, and escalation when boundaries are encountered.
